title: Sowing carrots
subtitle: Direct sowing from March to July for roots from June through autumn
excerpt: Carrots are sown direct into a fine, stone-free seedbed from March to July. They need no transplanting and very little attention between sowing and harvest. The challenge is thin sowing, a prepared bed, and keeping the carrot fly off.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden chapter. Gertrude Jekyll, Home and Garden (1900), Project Gutenberg. RHS carrot growing guide (rhs.org.uk). USDA agricultural extension service notes on carrot culture, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small fly (Psila rosae) whose larvae tunnel through carrot roots, leaving rusty brown trails. The fly lays eggs near carrots attracted by the smell of carrot foliage, especially when the crop is thinned. The main defences are a 60 cm solid barrier around the bed and avoiding thinning on still warm afternoons when the fly is most active.

Soil broken down to a crumb-like texture with no stones or large clods. Achieved by raking a well-dug or no-dig bed in dry conditions. Carrots need a fine tilth to germinate evenly and to produce straight, unforked roots; large stones deflect the taproot and cause forking.

content.text: Carrots go in direct from March to July in the UK, with each sowing ready to pull roughly three months later. The seed is tiny and slow to germinate; a
, thin sowing, and patience are what the crop asks for. Carrot fly is the main pest: a 60 cm barrier around the bed stops most of them.

The first outdoor sowing in most UK gardens is late March, once the soil reaches 7°C. Earlier sowings in February under cloches or fleece can work in a sheltered south-facing bed, but germination is slow and erratic if the soil is below 5°C. Maincrop varieties (those you want to leave in the ground and harvest through autumn) go in from April to mid-June. Early varieties (Amsterdam Forcing, Nantes) give a harvest from late June if sown in late March.

Full sun on a light, sandy, or well-worked loam. Remove stones and break up compacted soil before raking. If your soil is heavy clay or full of stones, consider growing short-rooted varieties (Chantenay, Paris Market) in a raised bed filled with a mix of compost and sharp sand. Deep, straight taproots form in deep, loose, stone-free soil; shallow or stony soil produces forked, distorted roots.

Draw a shallow drill 1 cm deep and sow seed as thinly as you can manage: ideally one seed every 2 to 3 cm. The seed is so small that most gardeners sow too thickly and then thin later. Rows 15 to 20 cm apart. Cover lightly, firm with the back of a rake, water gently.

Carrot seed germinates slowly: two to three weeks is normal in cold spring soil. In warm conditions (18-20°C) germination takes one to two weeks. Seedlings emerge as a single thread-like shoot with tiny ferny first leaves. If nothing shows after four weeks and the bed has been kept moist, the seed has failed; resow.
Once seedlings are 2 cm tall, thin to 5 cm apart. Thin again to 10 cm when plants are 10 cm tall. Do the final thinning in the evening, not on a warm afternoon, to reduce the smell that attracts

. Firm the soil back around remaining plants after thinning; exposed roots attract pests. A 60 cm solid barrier (fleece, clear polycarbonate, or fine mesh on stakes) around the bed excludes most carrot fly, which flies low.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: What breaks down most often with carrot sowing and growing.

items.cause: Stones or compacted soil in the bed, or fresh manure.
items.fix: Remove stones and break up the soil to at least 30 cm. Do not add fresh manure to a carrot bed; use only well-rotted compost worked in the previous autumn.

items.symptom: Rusty brown channels in the root flesh
items.fix: Put up the 60 cm barrier before the first sowing. Avoid crushing carrot foliage during weeding; the smell attracts the fly. Resistant varieties (Flyaway, Resistafly) show some tolerance.

items.cause: Slugs feeding on the tiny seedlings at night.
items.fix: Lay slug barrier (copper tape, wool pellets) around the bed at sowing time. Check under boards and pots near the bed at night.

items.symptom: Very uneven germination, bare patches in the row
items.cause: Dry surface soil crusting over and preventing seedling emergence.
items.fix: Water with a fine rose before and after sowing if the weather is dry. Lay a plank or fleece over the row until germination, then remove immediately. The shade keeps moisture in and softens the surface.
